en: During the day, land heats faster than the sea, causing warm air over land to rise and cooler ocean air to rush in, creating a sea breeze.
Earth's tilted axis causes the Northern Hemisphere to receive direct sunlight during summer, while the Southern Hemisphere receives slanted sunlight and experiences winter.
As the Moon orbits Earth, the changing angle of sunlight illuminating its surface causes us to see different shapes, creating the lunar phases.
The Moon's gravitational pull draws ocean water toward it, creating a tidal bulge that results in high tides on the side of Earth facing the Moon.
Slightly acidic rainwater dissolves underground limestone bedrock over thousands of years, carving out empty spaces that eventually form large caves.
When tectonic plates stuck together suddenly slip and release stored elastic energy, the resulting seismic waves shake the ground and cause an earthquake.
Heavy rainfall saturates soil on steep slopes, adding weight and reducing friction, which causes the loose earth to slide rapidly downhill.
Plant roots grow into tiny rock cracks and expand as they thicken, physically wedging the solid stone apart into smaller soil particles.
Gravity pulls clouds of hydrogen gas tightly together, heating the core until nuclear fusion ignites and a new star begins to shine.
The Sun heats ocean water into vapor that rises, cools in the upper atmosphere, and condenses around tiny dust particles to form clouds.
Magma trapped deep underground cools very slowly, allowing large mineral crystals to grow and form solid igneous rocks like granite.
Magma rises and releases dissolved gases that expand rapidly, building immense pressure until it violently blasts rock and ash out of a volcano.
